item.title: Pixels over Symbols: Sensory Realism Improves Behavioral Alignment in Models of Cognition
item.description:
Relevance: 35% | Source: arXiv AI
Hao Yuan Bai, Xiaoxuan Lei, Zihan Weng, Motahareh Pourrahimi, Lucas Gomez, Pouya Bashivan
arXiv:2611.10565v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computational models of cognition have traditionally relied on abstract symbolic inputs that approximate sensory experiences with simplified vector representations. This simplification reflects historical computational constraints and a long-held assumption that the details of sensory realism are incidental to the study of cognitive processes. Recent advances have enabled the development of sensory-realistic models capable of performing diverse cognitive tasks, yet whether sensory realism meaningfully shapes cognition has not been formally established. We address this gap through a large-scale empirical comparison of abstract and sensory-realistic neural network models trained on a battery of memory-dependent decision-making tasks. Our results show that sensory-realistic models mirror human behavioral response patterns significantly more than their abstract counterparts, though a substantial gap to human internal behavioral consistency remains even for the best tested models. By analyzing the internal dynamics of these systems, we find that the learned recurrent weights are not the main source of this divergence. In fact, frozen abstract-trained weights driven by sensory-realistic inputs recover the human consistency of sensory-realistic models. The resulting dynamics are also within the seed-to-seed variability of sensory-realistic models. Together, our findings argue that across a broad set of visual working-memory tasks, sensory realism accounts for a substantial portion of the model-human behavioral agreement, more than the choice of sequence architecture and comparable to the choice of vision encoder. These results suggest that findings obtained from abstract task models in neuroscience should be more carefully interpreted in light of their potential behavioral limitations.

item.title: Structure is in the zoom: probing neural symmetry through dimensionality scaling
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Adil Amin
arXiv:2611.08506v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling exponents of neural dimensionality are read as properties of the code, and used to compare representations and benchmark models against cortex. Yet one recording of 11,311 mouse V1 neurons gives 0.25, 0.30 or 0.35, depending only on how it is subsampled. We show that such an exponent measures the population and the probe together. We split it exactly into a floor, which random subsets of the same sizes give, and a shift, which a declared axis of stimulus classes adds. The usual random-subsample exponent is almost all floor. Stimulus direction lifts the exponent in every grating recording by reading both symmetry sectors of the code: orientation, which repeats every half turn, and direction, which does not. The lift lives in trial-to-trial fluctuations that differ between directions, while the class means, which linear decoders read, pull it down. Two measured terms, how much the classes' fluctuations overlap and how the means sit against them, account for the shift. They give its sign where it changes: in Allen Neuropixels recordings, whose class means mostly raise the exponent, and in macaque V1. In an XY lattice whose classes stay on one orbit, temperature flips the sign as the two terms say, and in GPT-2 the shift ranks the indirect-object circuit's name-mover and backup heads. Reported with its path, its floor and its shift, an exponent says how much structure a probe finds and what carries it. Our open tool, rung, reports all three for any labelled neural recording or language-model layer: https://github.com/adilamin89/structure-in-the-zoom

item.title: Brain-Aligned Latent Actions: Imposing Premotor Cortex Geometry on a Robot's Action Vocabulary
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Amit Jadhav
arXiv:2611.11674v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Robot policies increasingly act through a small vocabulary of discrete latent actions learned from unlabeled video, yet training leaves open which motion receives which code. We find this choice highly unstable: two independently trained runs of Moto's latent motion tokenizer assign the same robot clips to nearly unrelated codes (adjusted Rand index 0.001), and evaluating one tokenizer in bf16 instead of fp32 reassigns 74% of its tokens. We use this freedom to impose the representational geometry of macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv), recorded while a monkey drew shapes, on the tokenizer's code assignment, with a straight-through similarity loss trained alongside its reconstruction objective on robot video. In one training run per target, on five shape categories the loss never saw, the PMv-trained tokenizer reaches a representational similarity of 0.52 with PMv, against 0.20-0.26 for released and no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for the 95th percentile of random kinematic encoders. Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer (-0.17 to -0.03). Two results limit the claim: a hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv better (0.65), and a label-shuffled PMv control scores 0.41. We specify the downstream manipulation test, on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results, before running it.

item.title: Electrophysiological Dynamics of Default Network Suppression
item.description:
Relevance: 33% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Sun, W., Libowitz, M. R., Cowan, R. L., Tobel, T., Du, J., Feldman, D. A., Davis, T. S., King, J. B., Rahimpour, S., Smith, E. H., Buckner, R. L., Shofty, B.
Distributed brain networks compete with one another in the service of information processing. One dramatic example is antagonism between networks that support internally directed cognition, often collectively referred to as the default network, and networks that orient to external events and drive action. Here we combined within-individual precision functional neuroimaging and intracranial electrophysiology to investigate network competition at high spatiotemporal resolution. In six patients, robust antagonism between networks was established during a target detection task. Network-assigned electrophysiological recordings displayed concordant responses, including in single-neuron firing rates, and further revealed the temporal dynamics of network competition. Networks involved in salience detection and action planning showed early, transient responses that peaked near the participant response. Default network suppression occurred later, reflected in decreases in high-frequency broadband activity and in single-neuron firing rates in response to targets. Examining subcortical regions revealed rapid activity increases in the thalamus and posterior hippocampus aligned to the participant response. Critically, a late evolving, sustained suppression was observed throughout the hippocampus. These findings suggest that, across cortical and subcortical regions, network competition is temporally layered. Furthermore, the hippocampus can be dissociated along its long axis during competition. Such push-pull antagonism may be fundamental to advanced human cognition, and its disruption may underlie mental illness.

item.title: The neural circuit implementation of distributional reinforcement learning
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Matias, S., Rullan Buxo, C., Xu, S., Campbell, M. G., Lowet, A. S., Lu, X., Wu, Y., Schalek, R., Lichtman, J. W., Watabe-Uchida, M., Drugowitsch, J., Uchida, N.
Distributional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms outperform traditional RL by representing the full probability distribution of future outcomes rather than its mean. Neural signatures consistent with distributional coding have been observed in dopamine neurons and in striatal value representations. However, how distributional RL is implemented within the anatomical circuit organization of the basal ganglia remains unknown. Uncovering how representations of outcome distributions are organized across brain circuits has broad implications for both fundamental and clinical neuroscience, providing new insights into how the brain represents uncertainty and how these representations shape risk-sensitive learning and decision-making. Here, we investigated how representations of outcome distributions are organized across dopamine projections to the striatum by combining striatum-wide fiber photometry of dopamine axonal activity with Neuropixels recordings from projection-defined dopamine neurons. We found that distributional reward prediction error signals are preferentially encoded in lateral ventral striatum-projecting dopamine neurons, but that reward distribution information is shared between the ventral and the dorsal striatum. Additionally, an anatomical gradient of optimism in the midbrain supports the diversity of value predictions required for distributional RL. Our findings extend the actor-critic framework proposed for the basal ganglia by revealing distributional prediction errors in a subpopulation of mesolimbic dopamine neurons capable of training parallel striatal regions thought to implement different types of behavioral control.

item.title: Ergodic breakdown of brain dynamics under chronnectome complexity across cognitive states and age
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Kazemivash, B., Zhu, D.
Chronnectome complexity, the extent to which time-varying functional connectivity follows a structured sequence of distinct configurations, contributes to shaping large-scale brain dynamics. However, it remains unclear how this complexity influences the encoding of information that distinguishes resting state and task conditions. In ergodic theory, time averages represent ensemble behavior under ergodicity, which breaks down when dynamics are non-stationary, as when activity moves sequentially between distinct regimes. We hypothesize that this information resides in time-averaged connectivity under lower-complexity conditions but in trajectory geometry under higher-complexity conditions, where brain activity traverses distinct configurations over time, consistent with ergodic breakdown, which we term the textit{information migration principle}. We formulate this as dynamics-driven multi-class classification and introduce the Brain Dynamics Classifier (BDC), an interpretable data-driven mechanistic model in which a graph neural network embeds dynamic functional connectivity into a latent space and a neural ordinary differential equation learns the vector field governing trajectories through that space. The proposed model derives two complementary representations within a single learned dynamical system, capturing time-averaged connectivity, which is sufficient under ergodic dynamics, and trajectory geometry, which preserves the temporal organization obscured by averaging under non-ergodic dynamics. Our results show high classification accuracy, $97.4%$ for eight conditions in the Human Connectome Project young adult cohort and $92.2%$ for four in the aging cohort. To test the information migration principle, we ablated the time-averaged representation and found that trajectory contributions varied with chronnectome complexity, from high for Working Memory to absent for Relational Reasoning, consistent with ergodic breakdown. Including subcortical regions further increased trajectory contributions for affective conditions. In aging, the distinction between higher and lower complexity conditions was preserved, resting-state dynamics became less ergodic with advancing age, and higher fluid intelligence was associated with more ergodic resting-state dynamics.

item.title: Subliminal Learning Is Steering Vector Distillation
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv AI
Camila Blank, Agam Bhatia, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Arthur Conmy, Neel Nanda
arXiv:2606.00995v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Subliminal learning refers to a student language model acquiring a teacher's traits (e.g. a system-prompted preference for owls) when fine-tuned on the teacher's outputs, despite the outputs being semantically unrelated to those traits. It remains poorly understood how data without semantic meaning can transfer specific semantic traits. In this work, we show that subliminal learning is mediated by a single steering vector, i.e. a vector added to the model's activations. Across two open-source models, we find that the teacher's system prompt is well approximated by a steering vector, and that the student's behavior is driven by learning an aligned vector over fine-tuning. System prompts that are not well approximated by steering vectors are not subliminally learned. This is a special case of steering vector distillation, in which a student trained on the outputs of a steered teacher learns to imitate that steering. We demonstrate steering vector distillation on a range of semantic and random vectors. Adding a semantic vector to a model's activations can have both model-independent and model-specific (i.e. non-semantic) effects on its behavior, so generated data that is non-semantic can transmit a vector with semantic effects, enabling subliminal learning. This also explains why subliminal learning does not transfer between models. We find that adaptive optimizers are necessary for subliminal learning in language models: activation gradients on steered data carry a small but consistent component along the steering direction, and non-adaptive optimizers impede this by allowing outlier gradients to dominate.

item.title: A Hierarchical Tokenization Framework for Voxel-Level fMRI Representation Learning
item.description:
Relevance: 32% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Karanpartap Singh, Yue Zhao, Mohammad H. Abbasi, Ehsan Adeli
arXiv:2611.11081v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce HBAR (Hierarchical Brain Activity Representation), a hierarchical tokenization framework for learning compact, multi-scale representations of neuroimaging data. HBAR organizes voxel-level resting-state fMRI into a hierarchy spanning sub-parcel voxel groups, parcels, and large-scale functional networks, enabling up to 415x compression while preserving fine-grained spatial information beyond conventional parcellation. The framework supports fixed atlas-based, fully learned, and softly prior-guided hierarchies, allowing us to systematically study the role of structured priors in brain representation learning. On HCP-YA, at approximately 415x compression, HBAR achieves higher parcel and network correlations than rate-matched flat tokenizers, while at a lower 52x compression rate, shuffling the anatomical grouping reduces parcel correlation from 0.920 to 0.886. Demographic readouts with autoregressive training also reveal potential gains from the hierarchical structure. By combining sub-parcel inputs, compact discrete tokens, and multiscale brain structure, HBAR offers a practical framework for representation learning in high-dimensional neuroimaging data.

item.title: Autonomous Continual Learning and Knowledge Transfer via Cortex-Inspired Neural Assemblies
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Kevin L. McKee
arXiv:2611.11717v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Unlike the brain, artificial neural networks (ANNs) suffer from "catastrophic forgetting": complete overwriting of solutions when re-training on new functions ("concept shift") or on a disjoint domain of the current function ("domain shift"). ANNs require each batch of data to be roughly representative of the complete distribution, a typically expensive and impractical requirement. In this paper, we introduce Functional Task Networks (FTNs), a method of continual learning and knowledge transfer modeled after several properties of the mammalian neocortex. FTN is formulated as a distributed, stochastic mixture of experts in which a sparse, binary routing mask is computed at inference time using a small support sample of input-output pairs. Per-batch reconfiguration of the router during training, together with mask-overlap-filtered replay, shapes a basis of overlapping, partially trained subnetworks. Unrelated tasks route through mostly separate assemblies, related tasks overlap on shared components. On block-sequentially trained continual learning and knowledge transfer tasks FTN retains solutions nearly as well as disjoint-mask isolation and attains the lowest pre-update head-start loss among matched-architecture comparators. The learned mask-overlap geometry tracks the known concept-sharing structure where available. We show experimentally that under correlated concept shift, support-set mask reconfiguration is necessary even for retention. Under domain shift, the distributed bank with replay is sufficient to handle retention without the configurer. Forward transfer, or head-start, and backward transfer, are also contributed by support-set mask configuration.

item.title: Learn from your own latents and not from tokens: A sample-complexity theory
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv Machine Learning
Daniel J. Korchinski, Alessandro Favero, Matthieu Wyart
arXiv:2605.27734v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative models, from diffusion models to large language models, achieve remarkable performance but at a cost in training data orders of magnitude larger than what biological learners require. An alternative paradigm has emerged in which networks are trained to predict their own latent representations of related views or masked regions, as in data2vec and JEPA -- an idea related to predictive-coding accounts of the cortex. Despite strong empirical results, the theoretical understanding of these methods remains limited. Central questions include: by how much does latent prediction actually improve data efficiency? Is there a benefit to stacking such methods into multi-scale hierarchies? We answer both using as data a tractable probabilistic context-free grammar that captures the compositional structure of natural language and images. Such a grammar generates strings of visible tokens by recursively applying production rules along a tree of hidden symbols of depth $L$. For such data, supervised or token-level SSL require a number of samples exponential in $L$ to recover the latent tree; we prove that latent prediction achieves this with a number of samples constant in $L$, up to logarithmic factors. We confirm this bound with (i) a hierarchical clustering algorithm, (ii) an end-to-end neural network whose predictor-clusterer modules predict their own latents at each level via gradient descent, and (iii) the first sample-complexity analysis of data2vec, which we show implicitly performs hierarchical latent prediction. This suggests that explicit stacking such as H-JEPA is largely redundant.

item.title: Unified Factored Representations Resist Catastrophic Forgetting
item.description:
Relevance: 31% | Source: arXiv AI
Joel Lehman, Kenneth O. Stanley
arXiv:2611.11020v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper explores an unexpected connection between the quality of a neural network's (NN's) internal representation and its vulnerability to catastrophic forgetting. The representational forgetting hypothesis is that networks with unified, factored representation (UFR) can resist catastrophic forgetting without any modification to the underlying fine-tuning algorithm or network architecture. The key insight is that catastrophic forgetting may largely result from fractured entangled representation (FER): fine-tuning on only part of the input domain results in disruptive changes for other input patterns, because of how individual features are globally entangled. In contrast, if a gradient update is compatible with how a UFR network factors its representation, such an update may result in coordinated change across the input domain, alleviating catastrophic forgetting. Experiments in two domains provide evidence for this hypothesis: (1) an illustrative 1D regression task, in which UFR networks constructed by hand are compared against networks trained from scratch with SGD, and (2) an image-regression task with NNs previously shown to exhibit UFR. In both settings, UFR networks forget substantially less than their FER counterparts when repeatedly fine-tuned on UFR-compatible variations. Further experiments show that a training loss that distills UFR representations into fresh NNs reduces forgetting; along with several additional controls, these results help isolate representation as the critical factor. Together these results suggest that representational quality is an underappreciated contributor to catastrophic forgetting, and that the encouragement and maintenance of such quality may require attending to what patterns a particular NN is ready to learn.

item.title: On Agentic Behavioral Modeling
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Dirk Ostwald, Rasmus Bruckner, Franziska Us\'ee, Belinda Fleischmann, Joram Soch, Sean Mulready
arXiv:2604.27894v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Integrating theoretical neuroscience, decision theory, and probabilistic inference offers a promising route to understanding human cognition, yet concrete methodological bridges between agentic artificial intelligence (AI) models and behavioral data analysis remain formally underdeveloped. We advance this synthesis within the framework of agentic behavioral modeling (ABM), which treats artificial agents as latent, generative hypotheses about cognitive mechanisms and evaluates them by their statistical adequacy in explaining human behavior. After outlining its conceptual foundations, we apply the framework to two minimal laboratory paradigms: a binary perceptual contrast-discrimination task and a symmetric two-armed bandit learning task. We formalize each task-agent-data system as a joint probability model, derive explicit conditional log-likelihoods for behavioral inference, validate different model variants using model and parameter recovery simulations, and evaluate them in light of empirical data. Using these minimal examples, we provide a novel agent-centric interpretation of the psychometric function, derive optimal policies for both tasks under explicit assumptions on sensory bias and post-decision noise, and show that the Bayesian posterior expectation and induced decisions admit an equivalent adaptive-rate Rescorla-Wagner representation in the symmetric bandit task. More broadly, this work may serve as a conceptual and practical foundation for applying ABM to cognitive behavioral science.

item.title: The Lagrangian Brain: A Constraint Mechanics of Mind and Machine
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv AI
Yuhang He, Si Wu
arXiv:2611.10737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A brain is in one state at a time, yet most of what decides its next state is absent from it: the patterns its world never produces, the statistics of a lifetime, a goal that lies ahead. In mechanics a wire acts on a bead only through a force that appears when the bead presses on it, and Lagrange computed such forces with one multiplier for each constraint. We propose that a brain follows the same mechanics. Everything a circuit knows, is told or wants is a constraint on its single state and acts through its own multiplier, which accumulates the violation and pushes the state back. Neurons and synapses carry the multipliers, each with its own time constant: inhibitory interneurons carry what never happens, adaptation the cost of staying in one state, synapses the statistics of experience, and feedback to apical dendrites the future. From this hypothesis follow Dale's law, the reciprocal wiring and balance of excitation and inhibition, the paradoxical responses of cortex and the frequencies of brain rhythms. Belief becomes the time one trajectory spends in each state, learning becomes sleep proposing laws and waking refuting the false ones, and planning becomes a wave from the goal meeting a wave from the present. Connectionism and symbolism are the limits of frozen and of instantaneous multipliers, and between them the time a circuit runs becomes the depth of its computation. A machine built on these principles, trained without gradients on 1000 solved puzzles, solves all 422,786 Sudoku-Extreme test puzzles with one trajectory each. It rediscovers the rules of Sudoku by sleeping and waking, plans shortest paths in mazes of 64 times the training area, and tracks permutations exactly on strings 25 times longer than in training, where Transformers fail. A mind, on this view, is life that learns its own constraints.

item.title: Learning Reusable Behavioral Motifs for Continuous Animal Behavior Modeling
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Jiyi Wang, Jingyang Ke, Bo Dai, Anqi Wu
arXiv:2506.15190v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Natural behavior evolves continuously and often reuses movement structure across contexts, but existing behavioral segmentation methods typically assign a single discrete syllable at each time point or impose restrictive generative assumptions. We introduce Motif-based Continuous Dynamics (MCD), a computational framework that models behavior as time-varying combinations of reusable behavioral motifs. MCD learns motifs as latent behavior-level features from transition dynamics, through spectral representation learning within a reinforcement learning framework. MCD then infers policies that combine these motifs across time or context, through offline imitation learning. This formulation avoids hard behavioral boundaries while capturing continuity and compositionality. Across simulated gridworld and continuous-control tasks, mouse maze navigation and pose data, MCD identifies reusable motifs that explain task and temporal variation. MCD therefore provides a flexible and interpretable framework for computational behavior analysis. Code is available in https://github.com/G1NO3/MCD.

item.title: INTENSE: Information-theoretic discovery of behavioral selectivity of neurons in calcium imaging data
item.description:
Relevance: 30% | Source: arXiv Neurons and Cognition
Nikita Pospelov, Viktor Plusnin, Olga Rogozhnikova, Anna Ivanova, Vladimir Sotskov, Ksenia Toropova, Olga Ivashkina, Vladik Avetisov, Konstantin Anokhin
arXiv:2603.04622v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Neurons in freely behaving animals exhibit selectivity for diverse variables. Calcium imaging makes this selectivity hard to read out: behavioral variables covary, and fluorescence is slow and autocorrelated. We introduce INTENSE (INformation-Theoretic Evaluation of Neuronal SElectivity), an open-source framework that screens every neuron against all measured variables on a common statistical scale. INTENSE applies mutual information directly to fluorescence to detect relationships missed by linear correlation, optimizes neural-behavioral delays, performs autocorrelation-preserving circular-shift tests and examines whether apparent mixed selectivity reflects behavioral covariance. In ground-truth simulations, it reduced false associations caused by temporal structure and recovered more true associations than correlation-based screening. In CA1 recordings from 16 freely exploring mice, INTENSE identified neurons selective for position, head direction, object interaction and locomotor state. Accounting for correlated variables reclassified a large fraction of apparently mixed-selective neuron-session observations. INTENSE turns neural and behavioral recordings into testable maps of neuronal selectivity.

item.title: Accessing Mesoscale Functional Organization from Standard Functional MRI Leveraging AI-Based Super-Resolution
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Nasr, S., Li, H. B., Zemlyanker, D., Huber, L., Rosen, M. S., Iglesias, J. E.
Access to the fine-scale functional organization of the human brain is essential for understanding cognition and neurological disorders yet remains beyond the reach of conventional functional MRI (fMRI) because of its limited spatial resolution and contrast-to-noise ratio. To overcome this limitation, we developed f-LENNS (functional Localization Enhancement via Neural-Net-Sharpening), an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework that enhances the effective spatial resolution of reconstructed fMRI magnitude images. The model was trained exclusively on high-resolution synthetic MRI data using extensive domain randomization and no adversarial or generative components. This approach enables robust out-of-the-box generalization (without retraining) to experimental datasets obtained with diverse acquisitions, while effectively curbing hallucination. Our experiments show that our publicly available model substantially improves the spatial fidelity of functional activation maps across multiple imaging paradigms and generalizes to a cohort of individuals with atypical brain function caused by amblyopia (lazy eye). F-LENNS consistently outperforms conventional resolution enhancement approaches, including interpolation-based upsampling and sharpening methods. These findings demonstrate that AI-driven super-resolution combined with domain randomization can overcome domain shifts arising from differences in MRI acquisition, enabling scalable, fine-scale functional brain mapping with widely available MRI hardware.

item.title: Distinguishing evidence accumulation from choice confidence in neural signatures of perceptual decision making
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: bioRxiv Neuroscience
Monakhovych, D., Grogan, J. P., Kelly, S. P., O'Connell, R. G.
Human electrophysiology research has identified the centro-parietal positivity (CPP) as an apparent neural correlate of sensory evidence accumulation during perceptual decision-making. The CPP has also been shown to closely scale with subjective confidence. Coupled with the fact of its domain-generality and lack of choice selectivity, this observation raises the possibility that the CPP might in fact trace subjective confidence rather than cumulative evidence, two quantities that are closely correlated in most experiments. To disentangle confidence from cumulative evidence, we used predictive cues with 80% validity to manipulate prior expectations of participants during a contrast discrimination task while recording electroencephalography (EEG). At the time of decision termination, confidence is expected to reach a higher level for validly cued versus invalidly cued choices, whereas the opposite would be expected of a cumulative evidence signal due to biased decision starting points. As expected, valid cues led to faster, more accurate and more confident responses compared to invalid and neutral cues. At the neural level, cues produced systematic increases in preparation of the expected action prior to evidence onset as indexed by premotor mu/beta activity, consistent with cue-biased criterion adjustments. The pre-response CPP amplitude was significantly reduced for validly cued choices and the effect remained even when matching for confidence. Together these findings suggest that the CPP is not a direct read-out of subjective confidence, but an evidence accumulation signal that contributes to both decision formation and confidence estimation.

item.title: What's Holding Back Latent Visual Reasoning?
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv AI
Andr\'e G. Viveiros, Nuno Gon\c{c}alves, Andr\'e F. T. Martins, Matthias Lindemann
arXiv:2605.18445v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Humans can approach complex visual problems by mentally simulating intermediate visual steps, rather than reasoning through language alone. Inspired by this, several works on Vision-Language Models have recently explored chain-of-thought reasoning with continuous latent tokens as intermediate visual imagination steps. In this work, we investigate how recent models leverage such latent tokens. Surprisingly, we find that model accuracy is unaffected when latent tokens are replaced by uninformative dummy tokens. This indicates that latent tokens play a minimal causal role in the model's final prediction. To better understand this phenomenon, we analyze both the training signal provided by oracle latent representations and the quality of the latent tokens generated at inference time. Our experiments reveal two crucial issues holding back latent visual reasoning: First, in most existing datasets, oracle latent tokens provide limited additional information beyond the original image and do not substantially simplify the task, leading models to ignore them during training and effectively bypassing them at inference time. When fine-tuned on a diagnostic dataset, in which latent tokens provide sufficient support for the final prediction, we show that models can causally rely on them. Second, the latent tokens produced at inference time deviate from their corresponding oracle representations, collapsing to a narrow region and preventing benefits even when the model relies on them. Overall, our findings suggest that future progress in latent visual reasoning depends on two key pillars: high-quality datasets with informative intermediate steps and more precise latent token prediction.

item.title: Perception, Not Reasoning, Limits Visual Theory of Mind
item.description:
Relevance: 29% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Mohamed Rayan Barhdadi, Syed Talal Wasim, Juergen Gall, Erchin Serpedin, Hasan Kurban
arXiv:2611.10694v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models pass text-based false-belief probes at near-human levels but drop by over twenty percentage points on abstract panels the moment the same problem is conveyed visually. The consensus diagnosis is conceptual, prescribing new belief-reasoning modules. We argue the dominant bottleneck is perceptual: not what the model cannot reason about, but what it cannot see. We propose a five-condition dissociation protocol that holds the reasoning task constant while varying perceptual fidelity from visual only to text only, and quantify the result with the Perceptual Contribution Ratio, the share of the visual-to-text gap a given fidelity closes. We test this on two kinds of scenes: abstract 2D panels in the Heider--Simmel tradition, and naturalistic 3D game scenes from MuMA-ToM and MindPower. The evaluation covers seven VLMs and roughly 159,000 API calls. Ground-truth scaffolds substantially close the gap in every setting, and on the abstract panels and MuMA-ToM they match or exceed the text-only reasoning. Whereas scaffolds built by automatic parsers, including frontier VLMs, fail. The most common error in the visual-only condition is \emph{reality bias}, which accounts for 60\% of false-belief failures. Models report where an object actually is, not where an absent agent believes it is. This points to a perceptual front-end that fails to track which agents were present at each moment. Under the evaluated protocol, structured visual scene-state extraction, rather than belief inference, is the dominant bottleneck for visual ToM.

item.title: Focus Matters: Attention-Value Dynamics for Efficient Hallucination Mitigation in Vision-Language Models
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Sohyeon Kim, Sang Yeon Yoon, Kyeongbo Kong
arXiv:2604.03556v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved impressive progress in multimodal reasoning, yet they remain prone to object hallucinations, generating descriptions of objects that are not present in the input image. In this work, we investigate hallucination from the perspective of attention-value dynamics inside LVLM vision encoders. We identify a consistent three-phase structure of visual processing---diffusion, focus, and rediffusion---and show that the focus phase is where attention most clearly separates strongly and weakly supported visual tokens. However, low attention does not necessarily imply negligible downstream influence: low-attention tokens in the focus phase can still exert non-negligible value-side influence on the attention output relative to their small attention mass. Through controlled phase-wise value interventions, we find that hallucination behavior is particularly sensitive to the value content of low-attention tokens during this phase. Replacing or neutralizing these values reduces hallucination metrics while largely preserving grounded object evidence. A token-level teacher-forcing analysis further shows that the intervention reduces the probability of hallucinated object tokens with much smaller effects on ground-truth object tokens. In addition, Visual Attention Ratio (VAR) analysis shows that focus-phase intervention is accompanied by increased attention to visual tokens during decoding. Based on these observations, we instantiate a simple training-free inference-time intervention that replaces focus-phase low-attention values with an image-level mean value vector using statistics from a single forward pass. Experiments across multiple LVLM backbones demonstrate that this analysis-derived intervention reduces object hallucination with negligible additional runtime and remains compatible with existing inference-time mitigation methods.

item.title: Task Vector Geometry Underlies Dual Modes of Task Inference in Transformers
item.description:
Relevance: 28% | Source: arXiv Computation and Language
Hao Yan, Haolin Yang, Yiqiao Zhong
arXiv:2605.03780v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transformers are effective at inferring the latent task from context via two inference modes: recognizing a task seen during training, and adapting to a novel one. Recent interpretability studies have identified from middle-layer representations task-specific directions, or task vectors, that steer model behavior. However, a lack of rigorous foundations hinders connecting internal representations to external model behavior: existing work fails to explain how task-vector geometry is shaped by the training distribution, and what geometry enables out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. In this paper, we study these questions in a controlled synthetic setting by training small transformers from scratch on latent-task sequence distributions, which allows a principled mathematical characterization. We show that two inference modes can coexist within a single model. In-distribution behavior is governed by Bayesian task retrieval, implemented internally through convex combinations of learned task vectors. OOD behavior, by contrast, arises through extrapolative task learning, whose representations occupy a subspace nearly orthogonal to the task-vector subspace. Taken together, our results suggest that task-vector geometry, training distributions, and generalization behaviors are closely related.

item.title: The Effect of Uncontrollable vs. Controllable Acute Stress on Inhibition as a boundary condition: A Replication and Extension of Starcke et al. (2016)
item.description:
Relevance: 26% | Source: SocArXiv
Yağız Benli
Executive functions (EF) are as set of higher-order, goal directed mental processes that enable individuals to focus, inhibitate, regulate their behaviour and manage complex tasks, particularly in situations where automatic responses are not enough (Diamond, 2012, p.136). Miyake et al. (2000) propose that there are three core EFs, working memory, inhibitory control and the flexible shifting of attention and that these abilities are essential for performing goal-oriented behavior by integrating various streams of information. Also, these cognitive processes are dependent on prefrontal cortex, making them particularly vulnerable to disruption by phsiological and psychological states such as acute stress. However, as emphasized in a recent review by Plieger and Reuter (2020), emprical finding on stress and executive functioning remain complex, some studies report impairments, while others suggest improvements, largely depending on moderating variables such as task complexity and the type of the stressor. The authors argue that stress may not simply reduce cognitive capacity but may instead make the brain rely more on automatic responses to preserve energy under stress A meta analysis by Shields et al. (2016) supports the sensivity of EFs, though the effect are not uniform across all domains. They demonstrated that acute stress significantly impairs core executive fuctions, espacially working memory and cognitive flexibilty. The impact on inhibition is less straightforward and showed more nuanced pattern. While stress tends to impair cognitive inhibition, it may sometimes enhance response inhibition. Consistent with the impairment view, Starcke et al. (2016) used the Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test (PASAT-C) to induce acute stress and found that stressed participants performed significantly worse than the non-stressed participants on the Color-Word Interference Test (stroop), meaning that uncontrollable stress distort the ability to filter interference. However, the impairment observed by Starcke et al. (2016) might not be due to stress intensity alone, but rather the uncontrollable nature of the stressor (unavoidable aversive noise). Henderson et al. (2012) investigated this distinction and found that controllability is a key moderater. In their study, participants exposed to uncontrollable stress showed no relationship between stress and performance whereas those who learned to control the stressor showed reduced Stroop interference, meaning that realizing that they had control over the stressor improved their performance. This suggests that the perception of control buffers individuals against the effects of stress on executive funtions. In other words, when individuals percieve that they have some degree of control over a stressful stimulus, their cognitive functions are less disrupted. Furthermore, in line with the Hendorson et al. (2012), Gathmann et al. (2014) showed that in certain high-demand conditions, brain uses adaptive mechanisms to preserve performance. This adaptive mechanisms allow individuals to maintain acurracy in stressful situations. In this context, the impairment observed by Starcke et al. (2016) may be caused by the lack of perceived control in their stress manipulation. The primary motivation for this study is to resolve inconsistencies regarding the impact of acute stress on executive functions. While starcke et al. (2016) provided evidence that acute stress impairs inhibition, they used PASAT-C stress induction paradigm which is strictly uncontrollable stressor, leaving it unclear whether the observed impairment was driven by phsiological intensity of stress or the psychological state of helplesness. As highlightened by Plieger and Reuter (2020), identifying moderating factors such as controlability is essential when we try to understand the relationship between stress and executive functions. A clearer understanding of this relationship would lead to a better understanding of cognitive resilience. Therefore, this study aims to replicate the inhibitory impairment reported by Starcke et al (2016) while introducing “perceived controllability” as a manipulated boundary condition. To directly address the original study’s concern that the length of test battery may reduce the stress response over time, the current study will focus only on the Attention and Inhibition component (Stroop Test), administered immediately after the stress induction. By comparing an Uncontrollable Stress group, a Controllable Stress group and a Control group, present study aims to show distorting impact of acute stress on inhibitory performance is reduced when individuals believe they have some degree of control over the stressor.

item.title: The shape bias as a word learning strategy in children born preterm
item.description:
Relevance: 24% | Source: SocArXiv
Cecilia Zuniga-Montanez et al.
Language is fundamental for children's academic success and social development. Children born preterm often have smaller vocabularies than children born full-term. In other child populations with language problems, smaller vocabularies have been argued to be related to the absence of a common word learning strategy, the so-called ‘shape bias’, which is the tendency to extend names of objects (i.e., nouns) to other objects of similar shape. The current study will therefore investigate if preterm children show a shape bias and, if so, whether it is as strong as that of full-term children. Preterm children do not only differ from full-term children in terms of language development, but also in general cognitive development, which seem to be related to their language development (Benassi et al., 2016; Ross, Demaria, & Yap, 2017; Zuccarini et al., 2017), something also assumed to be the case for typical language development (Deák, 2014). A weaker shape bias in preterm children might therefore at least partly be due to a general cognitive delay. We will therefore investigate whether the groups differ in terms of shape bias after controlling for non-verbal control. Because the shape bias relies on children being able to categorise objects by shape, we will include a test of children's shape categorisation skill. We will investigate whether the strength of the shape bias is related to the strength of the shape categorisation skill and whether any differences shape categorisation skills between the groups can explain their shape bias differences in word learning. The shape bias has been argued to be developed in typically developing children once their vocabulary includes 50-100 nouns (Gershkoff-Stowe and Smith, 2004) and its strength seems to be related to noun vocabulary size and make-up (Perry & Samuelson, 2011). We will therefore investigate whether the shape bias is stronger in preterm children with larger noun vocabulary sizes. Again, we will also investigate whether such a relationship is present once non-verbal abilities have been controlled for. We will focus on comprehension vocabulary because production vocabulary can be affected by motor control problems in preterm children. Furthermore, this study will test whether gestational age predicts the strength of the shape bias in preterm children.
